64 dead, 58 injured in Spain train crash, local authorities say
The latest local government update confirms 64 dead, and 58 injured in today’s crash.
40 of the dead were travelling on the Iryo train, and 24 on the AVE high-speed train, it added.
Dozens also injured after high-speed train crash in Toledo province
 Updated 
From 
Key events
The Andalusian regional government has declared three days of mourning. “We are devastated,” its president, Juanma Moreno, said.
“All of Andalusia stands with the victims of this latest train accident,” he added.
Earlier today, the mayor of Seville, José Luis Sanz, also announced three days of mourning and suspended all official events.
Jakub Krupa
We are still expecting to hear from Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente shortly. I will bring you his comments when he shows up.
Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez is expected to travel to the scene of the crash later today.
The government said:
 “The President of the Government, @sanchezcastejon, is traveling to Urda to support the work of the emergency teams and convey his support to those affected and their families.
The priority is to attend to the victims and ensure the maximum coordination between administrations.”
Death toll from the train crash has gone up to 64, sources in the local government in Castilla la Mancha told RTVE, El País and Reuters.
It makes it a deadlier incident than this January’s Adamuz crash (11:00), and the third worst train disaster in Spain since the seventies (12:55).
The death toll is still likely to change.
Latest dramatic pictures from the scene show the scale of devastation and appear to show a piece of broken rail going through the roof of one of the affected trains.
Gwyn Topham
Transport correspondent
The signalling system used on the high-speed line between Madrid and Seville will come under scrutiny as investigators seek to understand Spain’s latest horrific rail crash.
The rear-end collision between two trains, whose death toll already looks likely to exceed the disaster in Adamuz on the same line in January, should, theoretically, be a remoter risk than other types of accident.
The LZB signalling system should automatically stop a train if the line ahead is occupied, even if the driver failed to apply the brakes.
The technology, used previously in Germany before being installed on the Spanish high-speed line, translates as “linear train control” and uses continuous electronic communication between the track and train to control speeds.
That should make it safer than, for example, the stretch of the Midland main line in the UK where a rear-end collision occurred earlier this year – the first fatal crash of its type between two passenger trains in Britain for more than 40 years.
In that part of the railway, there was no technology to automatically stop the second train, whose driver failed to apply the brakes when passing a red light that warned of danger ahead.
Spain has had another high-speed disaster, in Galicia in 2013, under a system where the driver was able to ignore speed warnings.
This should not have been possible under this system – a different scenario for investigators than the faulty rails identified in the head-on Adamuz crash.
According to early, unconfirmed reports from Spain (12:30), the first train, an Iryo service, may have stopped after flagging a failure in the LZB system.
Spain, like all European operators of high-speed lines, is transitioning its various signalling systems to a standard ERTMS service.
We are expecting to hear from Spain’s transport minister Óscar Puente at the top of the hour, at 2pm local time (1pm UK).
Spain’s former labour minister Fátima Báñez was reportedly on one of the trains caught up in this morning’s crash.
Speaking just now on RTVE, Antonio Sanz, the Andalusia government’s emergency minister, confirmed she is believed to have been on board and has not yet been reached since the incident.
